newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Investors concerned about Philippine stability.
newsitem.headline: Investors concerned about Philippine stability.

text.p: The Philippines' Central Bank Governor has sought to allay international investors' concerns about political stability in the country after President Fidel Ramos steps down, saying that democracy had taken a firm hold.

In a report to Ramos on his recent trip to the United States and Europe, Gabriel Singson said he had told fund managers and investors that democratic mechanisms were in place and all prospective presidential candidates aspiring to succeed Ramos "have generally supported current economic reforms".
"Economic reforms are already deeply rooted and will be politically hard to reverse," added the report, which was released on Sunday.

Ramos, whose six-year term ends in June 1998, is barred from running for re-election by the constitution which limits a president to a single term. He has denied opposition allegations that he plans to change the constitution to allow him to remain in office until 2000.

Singson said International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials he met in New York pinpointed three areas in the economy which they said required "close follow-up to ensure sustained success" of the country's reform programme. These were the growing trade deficit, the future of a tax reform package still pending in Congress and "possible risks to the banking system due to excessive foreign borrowings and over-exposure to the real estate market".

He said he told IMF officials the Philippines' balance of payments position remained fundamentally sound. Growing remittances from Filipinos overseas, expected to reach around $7 billion this year, and private capital inflows were more than adequate to finance the deficit, he added.

Singson said he pointed out that the trade deficit, projected by economists to reach between $12 billion and $12.5 billion by the end of the year, did not reflect a loss of export competitiveness or excessive consumption.
"Capital goods imports, which will support future growth, are in fact behind rapid import growth," he added.
Singson said he told IMF officials that Philippine authorities were carefully watching banks' property exposure, given the fears that the country's property boom was rapidly running out of steam.
"We are satisfied that their exposures ... are well within acceptable norms," he said.
